claim: A nuclear retention signal (NRS) was inserted at the C-terminus of the Srsf1 genomic locus to create a mouse model expressing a nuclear-retained SRSF1 protein.
source: To create an in vivo mouse model expressing only a nuclear-retained SRSF1 protein, we inserted a potent nuclear retention signal (NRS) at the C-terminus of the Srsf1 genomic locus (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach used to generate the mouse model.

claim: The NRS sequence used is naturally present in the non-shuttling SR protein SRSF2.
source: This sequence is naturally present in the non-shuttling SR protein SRSF2 and when fused to SRSF1 prevents its shuttling when overexpressed (Cazalla et al., 2002; Maslon et al., 2014; Sanford et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-assisted strategy was used to introduce an NRS sequence, a small linker and a T7 tag at the C-terminus of the canonical SRSF1 isoform.
source: We designed a CRISPR/Cas9-assisted strategy in which an NRS sequence, a small linker and a T7 tag were introduced at the C-terminus of the canonical SRSF1 isoform (Sun et al., 2010; Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental method and references figures showing the strategy.

claim: The targeting approach minimizes perturbation of the N-terminal RRM domains of SRSF1 that are crucial for RNA recognition and splicing function.
source: This approach minimizes perturbation of the N-terminal RRM domains of SRSF1 that are crucial for RNA recognition and its function in splicing (Clery et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on RRM domain function.

claim: Srsf1NRS/NRS mice were born from Srsf1+/NRS intercrosses and survived postnatally to day 14.
source: In contrast to the completely penetrant early embryonic lethality of Srsf1-/- knockout mice (Xu et al., 2005), Srsf1NRS/NRS mice were born from Srsf1+/NRS intercrosses and survived postnatally to the point of genotyping (day 14) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript presents data on mouse survival and references a figure showing genotyping results.

claim: Srsf1-/- knockout mice exhibit completely penetrant early embryonic lethality.
source: In contrast to the completely penetrant early embryonic lethality of Srsf1-/- knockout mice (Xu et al., 2005), Srsf1NRS/NRS mice were born from Srsf1+/NRS intercrosses and survived postnatally to the point of genotyping (day 14) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Postnatal Srsf1NRS/NRS mice displayed overt phenotypic abnormalities from day 14 onwards.
source: However, postnatal Srsf1NRS/NRS mice displayed overt phenotypic abnormalities from this stage onwards (see later).
evidence: The manuscript describes observed phenotypes in the mice.

claim: Cytoplasmic functions for SRSF1 are mostly dispensable for embryonic development.
source: These findings indicate that the cytoplasmic functions for SRSF1 allele are mostly dispensable for embryonic development.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the viability data presented.

claim: The SRSF1-NRS fusion protein is expressed in all tissues and cell lines tested derived from homozygous Srsf1NRS/NRS mice.
source: We confirmed that the SRSF1-NRS fusion protein is expressed in in all tissues and cell lines tested derived from homozygous Srsf1NRS /NRS mice (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents western blot data showing protein expression.

claim: The SRSF1-NRS chimeric protein is retained in the nucleus.
source: We and others have previously shown that the SRSF1-NRS chimeric protein is retained in the nucleus (Cazalla et al., 2002; Lin et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Endogenous SRSF1-NRS protein was only detected in mouse nuclei but not in human nuclei in heterokaryon assays.
source: As expected, we observed that SRSF1-NRS protein was only detected in the mouse but not in human nuclei, confirming that it is indeed restricted to the mouse nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, lower panel).
evidence: The manuscript presents data from heterokaryon assays.

claim: T7-tagged WT-SRSF1 was present in recipient HeLa nuclei, demonstrating the innate shuttling activity of WT SRSF1.
source: As a positive control, we transiently expressed a T7-tagged WT-SRSF1 in mouse NSCs and clearly observed its presence in the recipient HeLa nuclei, underlining the innate shuttling activity of WT SRSF1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, upper panel).
evidence: The manuscript presents control data from heterokaryon assays.

claim: The SRSF1-NRS fusion protein expressed from the endogenous Srsf1 locus is restricted to the nucleus.
source: This confirms that our targeting strategy was successful and the resulting SRSF1-NRS fusion protein expressed from the endogenous Srsf1 locus is in fact restricted to the nucleus.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the heterokaryon assay data.

claim: Homozygous Srsf1NRS/NRS mice were on average 30% lighter in weight than littermate controls.
source: First, these knock-in mice were visibly smaller in size, including those that survived up to 7.5 months of age, being on average 30% lighter in weight than littermate controls (Student's t-test, p<0.0001), suggestive of a growth restriction phenotype (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents weight data with statistical analysis.

claim: Srsf1NRS/NRS mice display a growth restriction phenotype.
source: First, these knock-in mice were visibly smaller in size, including those that survived up to 7.5 months of age, being on average 30% lighter in weight than littermate controls (Student's t-test, p<0.0001), suggestive of a growth restriction phenotype (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the weight data.

claim: Srsf1NRS/NRS embryos at E13.5 are grossly phenotypically normal.
source: Srsf1NRS/NRS embryos were grossly phenotypically normal at this stage of development (Figure 2B), with no difference in embryo or placenta weights compared to their Srsf1+/+ (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript presents embryo data and images.

claim: There was no difference in embryo or placenta weights at E12.5 between Srsf1NRS/NRS and Srsf1+/+ mice.
source: Srsf1NRS/NRS embryos were grossly phenotypically normal at this stage of development (Figure 2B), with no difference in embryo or placenta weights compared to their Srsf1+/+ (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript presents weight data for embryos and placentas.

claim: The observed growth restriction does not arise from impaired embryogenesis or abnormal maternal nutrient transfer across the placenta.
source: These results indicate that the observed growth restriction does not arise from impaired embryogenesis or abnormal maternal nutrient transfer across the placenta, suggesting that postnatal growth is specifically affected in Srsf1NRS/NRS animals.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the embryo and placenta data.

claim: Postnatal growth is specifically affected in Srsf1NRS/NRS animals.
source: These results indicate that the observed growth restriction does not arise from impaired embryogenesis or abnormal maternal nutrient transfer across the placenta, suggesting that postnatal growth is specifically affected in Srsf1NRS/NRS animals.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the growth data.

claim: Half of the Srsf1NRS/NRS animals developed hydrocephalus by P14.
source: In addition to restricted growth, half of the Srsf1NRS/NRS animals developed hydrocephalus by P14.
evidence: The manuscript presents data on hydrocephalus incidence.

claim: No cases of hydrocephalus were observed in Srsf1+/+ or Srsf1NRS/+ littermates.
source: In contrast, no cases of hydrocephalus were observed in either the Srsf1+/+ or Srsf1NRS/+ littermates (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript presents data on hydrocephalus incidence in control mice.

claim: Hydrocephalus is caused by the accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid resulting in dilatation of brain ventricles and increased pressure on the surrounding brain tissue.
source: Hydrocephalus is caused by the accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) resulting in dilatation of brain ventricles and increased pressure on the surrounding brain tissue, which can lead to cranial doming during the perinatal period (McAllister, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Hydrocephalus can result in progressive brain enlargement, neurological dysfunction, seizures, and death.
source: As in humans, hydrocephalus can result in progressive brain enlargement, neurological dysfunction, seizures, and death.
evidence: The claim draws from established medical knowledge.

claim: Hydrocephalus can be caused by obstruction of the aqueducts or abnormal beating of cilia lining the brain ventricles.
source: Hydrocephalus can be caused by obstruction of the aqueducts or abnormal beating of cilia lining the brain ventricles, thus preventing CSF flow (Ibañez-Tallon et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Coronal sections of P14 brains showed dilation of brain ventricles and damage to surrounding neurons.
source: Although coronal sections of P14 brains showed dilation of brain ventricles and damage to surrounding neurons, we found no evidence of aqueduct obstruction even in most severe cases of hydrocephalus (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript presents histological data.

claim: No evidence of aqueduct obstruction was found even in most severe cases of hydrocephalus in Srsf1NRS/NRS mice.
source: Although coronal sections of P14 brains showed dilation of brain ventricles and damage to surrounding neurons, we found no evidence of aqueduct obstruction even in most severe cases of hydrocephalus (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript presents histological data.

claim: Ependymal and choroid plexus cilia are present in Srsf1NRS/NRS animals.
source: Here, ubiquitous expression of the ciliary reporter ARL13B-Cerulean allows for live imaging of all ciliary types and revealed that ependymal and choroid plexus cilia are present in Srsf1NRS/NRS animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data using a ciliary reporter.

claim: Srsf1NRS/NRS males presented sperm with abnormal head morphology.
source: In addition to hydrocephalus and growth restriction, Srsf1NRS/NRS males presented sperm with abnormal head morphology and a large proportion of immotile flagella (Figure 3C), whereas those remaining motile exhibited abnormal waveforms (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript presents sperm analysis data.

claim: A large proportion of sperm flagella in Srsf1NRS/NRS males are immotile.
source: In addition to hydrocephalus and growth restriction, Srsf1NRS/NRS males presented sperm with abnormal head morphology and a large proportion of immotile flagella (Figure 3C), whereas those remaining motile exhibited abnormal waveforms (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript presents sperm motility data.

claim: Motile sperm in Srsf1NRS/NRS males exhibited abnormal waveforms.
source: In addition to hydrocephalus and growth restriction, Srsf1NRS/NRS males presented sperm with abnormal head morphology and a large proportion of immotile flagella (Figure 3C), whereas those remaining motile exhibited abnormal waveforms (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript presents sperm motility analysis data.

claim: Electron microscopy analysis revealed ultrastructural defects in the motile ciliary axonemes of mTECs from Srsf1NRS/NRS mice.
source: Electron microscopy analysis also revealed ultrastructural defects in the motile ciliary axonemes of mouse tracheal epithelial cultures (mTECs) from Srsf1NRS/NRS mice, including lack of central pair complex (1/81), supernumerary central microtubules (10/81), or single outer microtubules (2/81) compared to control Srsf1+/+ cultures (one single outer microtubule out of n = 94) (Figure 5G; X2 of all microtubule defects < 0.001) (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript presents electron microscopy data with statistical analysis.

claim: Defects in the structure and/or function of motile cilia may underlie multiple postnatal phenotypes observed in Srsf1NRS/NRS animals.
source: Together these results suggest that defect in the structure and/or function of motile cilia may underlie multiple postnatal phenotypes observed in Srsf1NRS/NRS animals including growth arrest, hydrocephaly, and reduced fertility.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the combined phenotypic data.

claim: Primary mTECs were used to study the de novo production of multiciliated cells.
source: In order to investigate the mechanisms by which cilia motility is perturbed in Srsf1NRS/NRS animals, we used synchronized primary mTECs derived from sets of Srsf1NRS/NRS and Srsf1+/+ littermates to allow the stepwise study of the de novo production of multiciliated cells (Vladar and Brody, 2013), including number of cilia formed by centriole amplification as well as changes in cilia content (Oltean et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach.

claim: mTEC cultures faithfully replicate airway developmental programs during the course of a few weeks.
source: From progenitors bearing a single non-motile primary cilia to fully differentiated epithelial cells bearing hundreds of motile cilia, these cultures faithfully replicate airway developmental programs (Jain et al., 2010) during the course of a few weeks (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The production of multiciliated cells is not affected in Srsf1NRS/NRS mTEC cultures.
source: High-speed video microscopy and immunofluorescence of mTEC cultures during differentiation indicate that although the production of multiciliated cells is not affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), a significant proportion of cilia remain immotile in Srsf1NRS/NRS inserts until ALI13 (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging and quantification data.

claim: A significant proportion of cilia remain immotile in Srsf1NRS/NRS mTEC cultures until ALI13.
source: High-speed video microscopy and immunofluorescence of mTEC cultures during differentiation indicate that although the production of multiciliated cells is not affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), a significant proportion of cilia remain immotile in Srsf1NRS/NRS inserts until ALI13 (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript presents motility analysis data.

claim: Mutant motile ciliary bundles exhibit altered beat patterns in relation to control cultures at later stages.
source: Moreover, even at these later stages, mutant motile ciliary bundles exhibit altered beat patterns in relation to the control cultures, as illustrated by kymographs, ciliary beat frequencies (Figure 4D, E), and beat coordination between ciliary bundles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents motility analysis data including kymographs and beat frequency measurements.

claim: The motility defects observed in tracheal cilia are consistent with those observed in sperm flagella.
source: The motility defects observed in tracheal cilia are consistent with those observed in sperm flagella (Figure 3D), suggesting that shared molecular mechanisms underlie these abnormal traits.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation comparing data from different tissues.

claim: Srsf1+/+ induces the coordinated expression of multiple cilia-associated proteins during maturation with a greater amplitude than Srsf1NRS/NRS.
source: This shows that Srsf1+/+ induces the coordinated expression of multiple cilia-associated proteins during maturation with a greater amplitude than Srsf1NRS/NRS.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the proteomics data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: The major changes between Srsf1NRS/NRS and Srsf1+/+ proteomes involved downregulation of proteins with GO terms related to 'assembly of motile cilia'.
source: The major changes between Srsf1NRS/NRS and Srsf1+/+ proteomes involved downregulation of proteins with GO terms related to 'assembly of motile cilia' (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The manuscript presents proteomics data with GO term analysis.

claim: The affected proteins include dynein motor assembly factors (DNAAFs) and axonemal dynein motors (DNAHs), as well as Tektins and N-DRC components.
source: Interestingly, the affected proteins include dynein motor assembly factors (DNAAFs) and axonemal dynein motors (DNAHs), as well as Tektins and N-DRC components that are required for normal axoneme assembly and proper motility of mature ciliary bundles (Figure 4G).
evidence: The manuscript presents proteomics data identifying specific protein classes.

claim: The abnormal levels of motile cilia components found in Srsf1NRS/NRS proteomes are consistent with the observed ciliary dysfunctions and structural defects.
source: The abnormal levels of motile cilia components found in Srsf1NRS/NRS proteomes are consistent with the observed ciliary dysfunctions and structural defects observed by TEM (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation connecting proteomics data to phenotypic observations.

claim: A significant decrease of the same functional groups observed in tracheal proteomes was seen in Srsf1NRS/NRS testes at P22-23.
source: Indeed, a significant decrease of the same functional groups observed in tracheal proteomes was seen in Srsf1NRS/NRS testes (Figure 4H), broadly, motor assembly factors (DNAAFs), axoneme bending regulators (DRCs), and support protein (CFAPs, RSPHs, and Tektins) without broader developmental delays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents proteomics data from testes.

claim: SRSF1 is required during motile ciliogenesis.
source: Together these results support a general requirement for cytoplasmic SRSF1 during motile ciliogenesis.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined proteomics and phenotypic data.

claim: The viability of Srsf1NRS/NRS knock-in mice strongly suggests that SRSF1-mediated splicing was not grossly affected in the homozygous animals.
source: The viability of Srsf1NRS/NRS knock-in mice strongly suggests that SRSF1-mediated splicing was not grossly affected in the homozygous animals.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the viability data.

claim: Previous work using an exogenous SRSF1-NRS protein revealed that the nuclear splicing role of SRSF1 was essential and could be decoupled from its ability to shuttle.
source: In addition, previous work using an exogenous SRSF1-NRS protein revealed that the nuclear splicing role of SRSF1 was essential and could be decoupled from its ability to shuttle (Lin et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: There were no gross splicing changes induced by the presence of the NRS insertion in MEFs.
source: Pairwise comparisons of Srsf1+/+, Srsf1NRS/+, and Srsf1NRS/NRS MEFs demonstrated that there were no gross splicing changes induced by the presence of the NRS insertion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq splicing analysis data.

claim: Only 26 changes in splicing were observed considering ΔPSI => 0.2 (p <= 0.01) out of 65,318 transcripts analyzed.
source: Out of 65,318 transcripts analyzed, we observed only 26 changes in splicing considering ΔPSI => 0.2 (p <= 0.01), which is comparable to the number of changes between Srsf1NRS/+ and Srsf1+/+ MEFs.
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq splicing analysis data.

claim: Precluding the shuttling ability of SRSF1 preserves its splicing function.
source: This confirms that precluding the shuttling ability of SRSF1 preserves its splicing function.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the splicing analysis data.

claim: Shuttling SR proteins, including SRSF1, have been proposed to function in nuclear mRNA export through interactions with the export factor TAP/NXF1.
source: Shuttling SR proteins, including SRSF1, have been also proposed to function in nuclear mRNA export, through interactions with the export factor TAP/NXF1 (Hargous et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2003; Huang and Steitz, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The abundance of 121 and 57 mRNAs was decreased in the cytoplasm of Srsf1NRS/NRS MEFs and NSCs, respectively.
source: We found that the abundance of 121 and 57 mRNAs was decreased in the cytoplasm of Srsf1NRS/NRS MEFs and NSCs, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data from cytoplasmic fractions.

claim: There was no overlap between SRSF1 direct export targets identified in P19 cells and mRNAs that change in cytoplasmic abundance in Srsf1NRS/NRS MEFs and NSCs.
source: In previous work, 225 transcripts were identified as the direct export targets of SRSF1 in P19 cells (Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016); however, we found no overlap between those targets and mRNAs that change in this study.
evidence: The manuscript compares current data to previously published data.

claim: A nuclear-restricted SRSF1 does not compromise pre-mRNA splicing and is associated with relatively few changes in mRNA export.
source: Taken together, our data shows that a nuclear-restricted SRSF1 does not compromise pre-mRNA splicing and is associated with relatively few changes in mRNA export.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the RNA-seq data.

claim: The shuttling ability of SRSF1 is not required for embryonic development but becomes important in later postnatal stages.
source: The shuttling ability of SRSF1 is not required for embryonic development but becomes important in later postnatal stages (Figures 2 and 3), suggesting that the shuttling ability of SRSF1 becomes more important as cells differentiate.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the developmental data.

claim: Substantial changes in the association of mRNAs with polysomes were observed in Srsf1NRS/NRS NSCs and MEFs, with a much lower proportion of changes in ESCs.
source: This analysis revealed substantial changes in the association of mRNAs with polysomes in Srsf1NRS/NRS NSCs and MEFs, with a much lower proportion of changes in ESCs (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript presents polysome profiling data.

claim: 1077 genes (total of 1258) in NSCs were under-represented in the polysomal fractions of Srsf1NRS/NRS samples.
source: We found that 13 genes (total of 88) in ESCs, 1077 genes (total of 1258) in NSCs, and 464 genes (total of 733) in MEFs were under-represented in the polysomal fractions of Srsf1NRS/NRS samples, strongly suggesting that SRSF1 is directly involved in their translation.
evidence: The manuscript presents polysome profiling data.

claim: SRSF1 is directly involved in the translation of genes under-represented in polysomal fractions of Srsf1NRS/NRS samples.
source: We found that 13 genes (total of 88) in ESCs, 1077 genes (total of 1258) in NSCs, and 464 genes (total of 733) in MEFs were under-represented in the polysomal fractions of Srsf1NRS/NRS samples, strongly suggesting that SRSF1 is directly involved in their translation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the polysome profiling data.

claim: The observed translational changes are not restricted to lineage-specific transcripts but instead appear to correlate with ongoing differentiation programs or metabolic demands of each cell type.
source: Therefore, the observed translational changes are not restricted to lineage-specific transcripts but instead appear to correlate with ongoing differentiation programs or metabolic demands of each cell type.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the polysome profiling data across cell types.

claim: Differentiating cells such as NSCs and to a lesser extent MEFs require SRSF1 for the translation of a subset of mRNAs.
source: These results suggest that differentiating cells such as NSCs and to a lesser extent MEFs require SRSF1 for the translation of a subset of mRNAs.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the polysome profiling data.

claim: Changes in polysome profiling and RNA levels did not correlate in either MEFs or NSCs.
source: Changes in polysome profiling and RNA levels did not correlate in either MEFs or NSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The manuscript presents comparative analysis of polysome and RNA-seq data.

claim: Translational changes are a direct response to the loss of SRSF1 in cytoplasm rather than a consequence of altered transcription or mRNA export.
source: This indicates that translational changes are a direct response to the loss of SRSF1 in cytoplasm rather than a consequence of altered transcription or mRNA export.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the comparative analysis.

claim: Only a small fraction of differentially expressed splicing isoforms in the cytoplasm were found to be differentially translated.
source: Moreover, only a small fraction of differentially expressed splicing isoforms in the cytoplasm (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B) were found to be differentially translated (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The manuscript presents comparative analysis of splicing and translation data.

claim: The absence of SRSF1 from the cytoplasm has a major impact on translation.
source: Overall, these findings show that the absence of SRSF1 from the cytoplasm has a major impact on translation and that these changes are specific to the cell type even though they primarily affect non-cell-type-specific RNAs.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the polysome profiling data.

claim: Genes associated with spindle category were identified as translationally downregulated in Srsf1NRS/NRS NSCs.
source: From this analysis, we identified genes associated with spindle category as translationally downregulated in Srsf1NRS/NRS NSCs, which agrees with our previous findings in SRSF1-overexpressing 293T cells (Maslon et al., 2014) and with the reduced body size of Srsf1NRS/NRS animals.
evidence: The manuscript presents GO analysis of polysome profiling data.

claim: The functional category related to motile cilium was enriched among genes depleted from polysomal fractions of Srsf1NRS/NRS NSCs.
source: Interestingly, the functional category related to motile cilium was also enriched among genes depleted from polysomal fractions of Srsf1NRS/NRS NSCs (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript presents GO analysis of polysome profiling data.

claim: NSCs express a number of mRNAs encoding motile cilia-specific proteins that were downregulated in Srsf1NRS/NRS NSCs polysome fractions.
source: In addition, NSCs express a number of mRNAs encoding motile cilia-specific proteins and these were downregulated in Srsf1NRS/NRS NSCs polysome fractions (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript presents polysome profiling data for specific ciliary genes.

claim: Dynein axonemal assembly factors Dnaaf1/Lrrc50 and Dnaaf3 were under-represented in the heavy polysome fractions of Srsf1NRS/NRS cultures.
source: We observed that dynein axonemal assembly factors Dnaaf1/Lrrc50 and Dnaaf3, which are required for the functional assembly of axonemal dynein motors, as well as motor subunits themselves including those of both inner dynein arms (i.e., axonemal dynein heavy chain 7 [Dnah7a]) and outer dynein arms (i.e., dynein axonemal intermediate chain 2 [Dnai2]) were under-represented in the heavy polysome fractions of Srsf1NRS/NRS cultures.
evidence: The manuscript presents polysome profiling data for specific ciliary genes.

claim: Mutations in dynein assembly factors and motor subunits are found in patients with primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD).
source: Together, these proteins form the functional macromolecular motors that drive ciliary movement, many of which are found mutated in patients with congenital dysfunction of motile cilia, termed primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) (Loges et al., 2009; Loges et al., 2008; Mitchison et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The abundance of Dnaaf1 and Dnaaf3 mRNAs was not altered in the cytoplasm of Srsf1NRS/NRS cultures.
source: Importantly, the abundance of these mRNAs was not altered in the cytoplasm of Srsf1NRS/NRS cultures (Figure 5—source data 2), which was further confirmed by direct RT-PCR for Dnaaf1 and Dnaaf3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq and RT-PCR data.

claim: Cytoplasmic activities of SRSF1 are important for the execution of cilia motility programs.
source: We propose that cytoplasmic activities of SRSF1 are important for the execution of cilia motility programs, providing an extra regulatory level that will ensure responsive and scalable translation at the peak demand of assembly of the complex motile cilia machinery.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the combined data.

claim: The polysomal distribution of seven out of eight motility-related mRNA transcripts were decreased in Srsf1NRS/NRS testes.
source: Strikingly, we found that the polysomal distribution of seven out of eight of these motility-related mRNA transcripts were decreased in Srsf1NRS/NRS testes (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: The manuscript presents polysome shift qRT-PCR data from testes.

claim: Mouse testes require SRSF1 for the translation of a subset of mRNAs that encode components of the motile ciliary/flagella machinery.
source: These results demonstrate that mouse testes require SRSF1 for the translation of a subset of mRNAs that encode components of the motile ciliary/flagella machinery.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the testes polysome data.

claim: The Srsf1NRS/NRS mouse model mimics organismal and cellular phenotypes attributable to defects in motile cilia, similar to those observed in PCD patients.
source: In summary, we show that the Srsf1NRS/NRS mouse model mimics organismal and cellular phenotypes attributable to defects in motile cilia, similar to those observed in PCD patients.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the combined phenotypic data.

claim: Phenotypic changes in Srsf1NRS/NRS animals are consistent with a lack of SRSF1-mediated cytoplasmic activities that particularly impact on mRNAs relevant to the motile ciliary machinery.
source: These phenotypic changes are consistent with a lack of SRSF1-mediated cytoplasmic activities that particularly impact on mRNAs relevant to the motile ciliary machinery, in agreement with altered proteomes and axonemal ultrastructure changes observed in Srsf1NRS/NRS animals.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion integrating multiple data types.

claim: SRSF1 promotes translation of mRNAs encoding RNA processing factors and cell-cycle and centrosome-associated proteins.
source: Indeed, SRSF1 promotes translation of mRNAs encoding RNA processing factors and cell-cycle and centrosome-associated proteins (Fu et al., 2013; Maslon et al., 2014; Michlewski et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The post-splicing activities of shuttling SR proteins have physiological roles in a living organism.
source: Despite increasing evidence for post-splicing activities of shuttling SR proteins, their physiological roles in a living organism has remained enigmatic.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Abrogation of cytoplasmic SRSF1 function resulted in several deleterious phenotypes without affecting the nuclear roles of SRSF1.
source: In our model, abrogation of cytoplasmic SRSF1 function resulted in several deleterious phenotypes without affecting the nuclear roles of SRSF1.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings.

claim: This is the first demonstration that interfering with the nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling of an RBP has severe phenotypic consequences giving rise to perinatal phenotypes.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that interfering with the nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling of an RBP has severe phenotypic consequences giving rise to perinatal phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The lack of observed phenotypes in early development could be due to a more permissive shuttling of SRSF2 in pluripotent murine P19 cells.
source: An alternative explanation is that the lack of observed phenotypes in early development could be due to a more permissive shuttling of SRSF2 in pluripotent murine P19 cells, whereas shuttling is abolished upon differentiation (Botti et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is a speculative alternative explanation supported by citation.

claim: Multiple organs that depend on motile cilia were affected in Srsf1NRS/NRS animals.
source: Whilst we observed no gross phenotypes associated with defects in primary (immotile) cilia in Srsf1NRS/NRS animals, multiple organs that depend on motile cilia were affected.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the phenotypic observations.

claim: Motile cilia are essential for providing coordinated mechanical force to drive sperm movement or movement of fluids across tissues affecting brain ventricles, trachea, and spermatozoa.
source: Motile cilia are essential for providing coordinated mechanical force to drive sperm movement or movement of fluids across tissues affecting brain ventricles, trachea, and spermatozoa.
evidence: The claim draws from established biological knowledge.

claim: Cytoplasmic functions for SRSF1 are essential in vivo during motile cilia differentiation.
source: The constellation of phenotypes, abnormal ciliary ultrastructure, altered proteomes, and disrupted motility provide strong evidence that cytoplasmic functions for SRSF1 are essential in vivo during motile cilia differentiation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined data.

claim: Depletion of mitotic oscillator component CDK1 hinders differentiation of multiciliated ependymal cells at the stage of massive centriole production.
source: In particular, depletion of mitotic oscillator component CDK1, previously shown to be a direct target of SRSF1 translation (Maslon et al., 2014), hinders differentiation of multiciliated ependymal cells at the stage of massive centriole production (Al Jord et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the absence of cytoplasmic SRSF1, differentiation appeared to occur on time and give rise to appropriately long multiciliated bundles.
source: However, in the absence of cytoplasmic SRSF1, differentiation appeared to occur on time and give rise to appropriately long multiciliated bundles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents data on mTEC differentiation.

claim: Cilia motility and movement coordination were specifically compromised in Srsf1NRS/NRS mTECs.
source: However, cilia motility and movement coordination were specifically compromised, and protein levels of motile ciliary components were significantly reduced (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: The manuscript presents motility and proteomics data.

claim: During multiciliogenesis, cells transition from bearing a single primary cilium to hundreds of motile cilia requiring de novo synthesis of millions of motor subunits and motile ciliary components.
source: During multiciliogenesis, cells transition from bearing a single primary cilium to hundreds of motile cilia requiring de novo synthesis of millions of motor subunits and motile ciliary components in the correct stoichiometry within a short developmental window couple to ciliary elongation.
evidence: The claim draws from established biological knowledge about multiciliogenesis.

claim: Transcriptional regulators of multiciliogenesis affect hundreds of motile ciliary genes and lead to a drastic decrease in the production of ciliated bundles and cilia number per bundle.
source: Although a well-defined transcriptional code for induction of cilia motility exists, these transcriptional regulators of multiciliogenesis affect hundreds of motile ciliary genes (Lewis and Stracker, 2021) and lead to a drastic decrease in the production of ciliated bundles and cilia number per bundle (Gomperts et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Drosophila mRNAs encoding motile ciliary proteins are stored in large cytoplasmic granules until their translation is required in the growing sperm axoneme.
source: During spermatogenesis, Drosophila mRNAs encoding motile ciliary proteins are stored in large cytoplasmic granules until their translation is required in the growing sperm axoneme, possibly regulating their translation (Fingerhut and Yamashita, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: There is evidence of phase-separated cytoplasmic foci termed dynein axonemal particles (DynAPs) that contain assembly factors, chaperones, and axonemal dynein proteins.
source: In vertebrates, there is evidence of phase-separated cytoplasmic foci termed dynein axonemal particles (DynAPs) that contain assembly factors, chaperones, and axonemal dynein proteins, which may provide a favorable environment for their orderly assembly and final transport onto cilia (Huizar et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: SRSF1 could contribute to localized mRNA delivery and/or translation at cytoplasmic foci during motile ciliogenesis.
source: It is possible that SRSF1 could contribute to localized mRNA delivery and/or translation at these cytoplasmic foci. It could promote the formation of mRNPs that confine such regulated transcripts until a timely co-translational assembly of these large protein complexes is required during motile ciliogenesis.
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis based on the data.

claim: The lack of cytoplasmic SRSF1 led to a decreased polysomal association of a subset of mRNAs in Srsf1NRS/NRS NSCs.
source: We provided evidence showing that abrogation of the cytoplasmic function of SRSF1 led to a decreased polysomal association of a subset of mRNAs in Srsf1NRS/NRS NSCs, yet its impact on AS (nuclear function of SRSF1) or on the abundance of target mRNAs in the cytoplasm (mRNA export) was minimal.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the polysome profiling and RNA-seq data.

claim: mRNA translation is specifically debilitated when SRSF1 is absent from the cytoplasm.
source: This strongly suggests that mRNA translation is specifically debilitated when SRSF1 is absent from the cytoplasm.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the polysome profiling data.

claim: The lack of cytoplasmic SRSF1 had little effect on translation in ESCs, but it affected translation of over 1000 genes in NSCs.
source: We found that the lack of cytoplasmic SRSF1 had little effect on translation in ESCs, but it affected translation of over 1000 genes in NSCs.
evidence: The manuscript presents polysome profiling data across cell types.

claim: Human ESCs maintain low overall levels of translation, with a global increase in high polysomes upon differentiation towards neural lineages.
source: These results are consistent with findings that human ESCs maintain low overall levels of translation, with a global increase in high polysomes upon differentiation towards neural lineages (Blair et al., 2017) and thus suggest that SRSF1 participates in developmental programs that rely heavily on translational control.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: SRSF1 participates in developmental programs that rely heavily on translational control.
source: These results are consistent with findings that human ESCs maintain low overall levels of translation, with a global increase in high polysomes upon differentiation towards neural lineages (Blair et al., 2017) and thus suggest that SRSF1 participates in developmental programs that rely heavily on translational control.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the polysome profiling data in the context of previous findings.

claim: The lack of cytoplasmic SRSF1 leads to reduced mRNA translation with a particular impact on mRNAs related to cilia biogenesis and function of motile cilia.
source: Thus, the lack of cytoplasmic SRSF1 leads to reduced mRNA translation, with a particular impact on mRNAs related to cilia biogenesis and function of motile cilia broadly impacting development of sperm flagella, as well as in multiciliated tissues such as trachea.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the polysome profiling and proteomics data.

claim: CFAP44 is mutated in human male infertility and hydrocephaly.
source: Intriguingly, CFAP44 (Coutton et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2017), which is mutated in human male infertility and hydrocephaly, was recently found to be also an RNA-binding protein localizing to DynAPs (Drew et al., 2020), although whether it functions as an RBP in translational control of motile cilia assembly remains unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Syndesmos (SDOS, NUDT16L1) binds to and negatively regulates translation of mRNAs responsible for the biogenesis of primary cilia.
source: In contrast, Syndesmos (SDOS, NUDT16L1) was shown to bind to and negatively regulate translation of mRNAs responsible for the biogenesis of primary cilia (Avolio et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: SRSF1 is able to respond to metabolic demands of the cell needing to reshape its proteome during differentiation.
source: An intriguing possibility is that SRSF1 is able to respond to metabolic demands of the cell needing to reshape its proteome during differentiation.
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis based on the data.

claim: The presence of the splicing factor SRSF1 in the cytoplasm is essential for proper postnatal development.
source: In summary, we have developed the first mouse model that allowed us to assess the in vivo relevance of SRSF1 nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling (Figure 7). We conclude that the presence of the splicing factor SRSF1 in the cytoplasm is essential for proper postnatal development, and this is mostly due to the effect of SRSF1 in mRNA translation, which critically affects developmental programs and target mRNAs involved in motile cilia biogenesis and function.
evidence: The claim is a main conclusion of the study.
